# DutyBoard — provisioning runbook for an AI agent

You are being asked to set up DutyBoard on someone's own altengine account. This file is
the whole procedure. Follow it in order.

DutyBoard is a task board that agents and people share. Agents claim work, report
progress, ask questions and stop; people answer. https://www.dutyboard.com explains the
idea — this file is only about installing it.

The console at https://www.dutyboard.com/app is a static page that talks to YOUR user's
altengine directly. Nothing you provision here reports to dutyboard.com, and no DutyBoard
operator can read the boards you are about to create.

**If you can run a program on your user's machine, use it instead of this runbook.** The
`dutyboard` binary does every step below with one command, and upgrades an existing install
the same way:

```
alt install altlimit/dutyboard            # https://github.com/altlimit/alt — no sudo
ALTENGINE_KEY=ak_… dutyboard --provision-only
```

It finds a DutyBoard already in the organization or creates one, deploys the function and the
console (with a config pointing the console at that function), and checks `/health` reports
the version it deployed. The key needs the same access as below. Read on only when running a
program is not possible.


## What you need

The altengine MCP server connected: `https://api.altengine.net/mcp`.

Your user creates the key at https://console.altengine.net, and the part that matters is
the **MCP / AI agent access** block on the key form. Those toggles are off by default and
nothing here works without them:

| Toggle                  | Set to    | Why                                            |
|-------------------------|-----------|------------------------------------------------|
| Instances & data        | **Write** | create the instances, set their config, apply the access rules, create the account |
| Functions               | **Write** | deploy the state machine                       |
| Usage                   | None      | not used                                       |
| Live desktop inspection | None      | not used                                       |

**Write, not Full.** Full additionally lets a key DELETE an instance and everything it
holds, and nothing in this runbook deletes anything. The only reason to grant it is if you
also want to be able to undo the install (see the last section) — and that is a decision to
make deliberately, not to collect in advance because it was next to the one you needed.

Billing, members and key creation are never reachable over MCP at any level, so no setting
here exposes them.

If a tool comes back saying the credential "lacks 'write'", that block is the reason — it
is not a bug in the runbook, and no retry will fix it.

Then call `whoami` and tell your user which organization you are about to spend money in.
Instances count against a quota and against a bill. If more than one organization is
plausible, ask before creating anything.


## What you are building

Six instances and one function:

| service   | name              | what it holds                                  |
|-----------|-------------------|------------------------------------------------|
| auth      | `dutyboard-auth`  | your user's account. Nobody else's.            |
| datastore | `dutyboard`       | boards, duties, the decision log, agent tokens  |
| channel   | `dutyboard-live`  | live board updates                             |
| functions | `dutyboard`       | the state machine — every write goes through it |
| blob      | `dutyboard-files` | screenshots and recordings on a duty            |
| search    | `dutyboard-search`| finished work, so an agent can ask whether something was done before |

USE THESE EXACT NAMES. The function falls back to all five, so using them means there is
nothing to configure afterwards. If you must use different ones, you have to set matching
`DUTYBOARD_DATASTORE` / `DUTYBOARD_AUTH` / `DUTYBOARD_CHANNEL` / `DUTYBOARD_BLOB` /
`DUTYBOARD_SEARCH` env
values on the functions instance, and that is a step this runbook does not cover.


## Step 1 — create the instances

```
create_instance  service=auth       name=dutyboard-auth
create_instance  service=channel    name=dutyboard-live
create_instance  service=datastore  name=dutyboard
create_instance  service=functions  name=dutyboard
create_instance  service=blob       name=dutyboard-files
create_instance  service=search     name=dutyboard-search
```

If auth or channel come back refused with "must be created in the console", you are talking
to an altengine that predates their being creatable from here. Ask your user to make those
two in https://console.altengine.net — same names, no configuration — and carry on. Nothing
else about this runbook changes.

`ALREADY_EXISTS` means someone ran this before. Carry on; the instance you wanted is there.

**Note the `slug` on the functions response.** It is a random label, it is NOT the instance
name, and the function's public hostname is built from it:
`https://<slug>-fn.altengine.app`. If you lose it, `list_instances service=functions`
reports it too.


## Step 2 — the auth instance's sign-up form and origins

Try it yourself first. Read the config, then send it back changed — `patch_instance_config`
merges only at the TOP level, so a partial `settings` object would drop every field you did
not mention:

```
get_instance_config  service=auth  instance=dutyboard-auth
```

```
patch_instance_config  service=auth  instance=dutyboard-auth  changes={
  "settings": { ...everything get_instance_config returned under settings, plus:
    "allowSignup": false,
    "passwordlessEnabled": true,
    "allowedOrigins": ["https://www.dutyboard.com"]
  },
  "signup": {
    "identityField": "email",
    "fields": [
      { "key": "email", "type": "email",  "required": true, "label": "Email" },
      { "key": "name",  "type": "string", "required": true, "label": "Your name" }
    ]
  }
}
```

If that is refused with "auth config must be edited in the console", you are on an altengine
that does not expose it yet. Ask your user to set the same three things on `dutyboard-auth`
in https://console.altengine.net, and wait for them to confirm before going on — steps 4 and
6 both depend on it.

Either way, what matters and why:

- **`name` in the sign-up fields.** Not decoration: every duty, note and answer is stamped
  with its author's name from the token's claims, and without the field they are all stamped
  blank. You also cannot create their account in step 6 with a name the instance does not
  collect.
- **The origin.** Without it the console cannot call the auth instance from a browser at
  all, and the failure says only "failed to fetch". Use `https://www.dutyboard.com` unless
  your user serves the console themselves — then it is wherever THEY serve it from, here and
  in the function's CORS list in step 5. Getting this wrong is the single most common way an
  otherwise perfect install does nothing.
- **Sign-up off.** You create their account in step 6, so the public route is never needed.
  Leaving it on means anyone who finds the instance can open one and spend their quota.
- **Passwordless on.** It is how they will actually sign in — see step 6.


## Step 3 — datastore settings

```
patch_instance_config  service=datastore  instance=dutyboard
  changes={"autoId":"uuid","autoIndex":true}
```

**That is the whole of the datastore setup — do not create indexes.** A datastore query
must be index-served, and `autoIndex` does not merely permit an uncovered one: the first
query that needs an index creates it and retries, transparently, reporting it back under
`auto_indexed`. On a datastore this new the collections are empty, so each build writes
nothing and costs nothing. Declaring the ten indexes DutyBoard uses up front would be ten
tool calls that buy exactly one thing: not paying for a backfill later. There is no data to
backfill.

(The declared list lives in `backend/indexes.json` in the repo, which is how the
repo-based installer does it and the record of what the app asks the datastore for. It is
documentation, not a prerequisite.)


## Step 4 — what a browser may read

The console reads the datastore DIRECTLY with the signed-in person's token. These rules
are what stop it reading anyone else's rows.

```
auth_set_rules  instance=dutyboard-auth  access={
  "datastore:dutyboard": {
    "level": "read",
    "rules": { "_default": {
      "projects": { "read": { "any": [
        [{ "field": "owner_uid", "op": "=",  "value": "$auth.uid" }],
        [{ "field": "slug",      "op": "in", "value": "$auth.claims.boards" }] ] } },
      "duties":   { "read": { "any": [
        [{ "field": "owner_uid",  "op": "=",  "value": "$auth.uid" }],
        [{ "field": "project_id", "op": "in", "value": "$auth.claims.boards" }] ] } },
      "threads":  { "read": { "any": [
        [{ "field": "owner_uid",  "op": "=",  "value": "$auth.uid" }],
        [{ "field": "project_id", "op": "in", "value": "$auth.claims.boards" }] ] } },
      "agents":   { "read": { "any": [
        [{ "field": "owner_uid",  "op": "=",  "value": "$auth.uid" }],
        [{ "field": "project_id", "op": "in", "value": "$auth.claims.boards" }] ] } }
    }}
  }
}
```

Send it exactly. Four things are deliberate and all four matter:

- `level` is `read` and no collection has a `write` rule. Every write in DutyBoard is a
  state-machine transition that touches more than one collection at once — claiming a duty
  writes the duty and the agent row together — and a row rule can only scope ONE collection
  per request. So the browser reads, and posts every change through the function.
- `tokens` is absent. Agent credentials must be default-denied to browsers.
- `attachments` is absent. The rows are harmless but the files they name are private, and a
  browser that could read the rows would learn what exists without being able to open it.
- Each read is "rows you own, OR rows on a board in your `boards` claim". That claim is how a
  board's members read it. You do not set it: the function writes it when an owner adds a
  member, and the console asks the function to repair it before its first read. Do not
  simplify the rule to the owner branch alone, or shared boards open empty.

`auth_set_rules` REPLACES the whole access config. If the instance is not brand new, call
`auth_get_rules` first and merge.


## Step 5 — deploy the state machine

Fetch the bundle — one self-contained ES module, no imports to resolve:

```
GET https://www.dutyboard.com/board.js
```

It is the exact output of `npm run build:fn` in
https://github.com/altlimit/dutyboard, so your user can rebuild it from source and compare
if they would rather not trust a file from a website.

```
functions_deploy  instance=dutyboard  name=board  code=<the bundle>  activate=true
  grants={
    "datastore:dutyboard":   "full",
    "auth:dutyboard-auth":   "write",
    "channel:dutyboard-live":"write",
    "blob:dutyboard-files":  "full",
    "search:dutyboard-search":"full"
  }
```

The function name MUST be `board`. `api` is a reserved function name on a functions host
and the deploy will be refused.

Those grants are the blast radius, so they are the least each service needs:
`datastore` is `full` because deleting a board deletes its rows and delete sits above
write; `auth` is `write` because adding someone to a board sets the claim their browser's
reads are scoped by (verifying tokens alone would need only `read`); `channel` is `write` to publish
and mint subscribe tokens; `blob` is `full` because deleting an attachment must remove the
object, not just the row; `search` is `full` for the same reason, since deleting a board has
to remove its documents.

Then let the browser reach it:

```
patch_instance_config  service=functions  instance=dutyboard
  changes={"corsOrigins":["https://www.dutyboard.com"],"allowedHosts":[]}
```

Without an origin list the function sends no CORS headers at all, and every call from the
console fails in the browser while working perfectly from curl.


## Step 6 — your user's account, and the way into it

Sign-up is off, so create it directly. No email is sent.

```
auth_create_user  instance=dutyboard-auth
  fields={"email":"<their email>","name":"<their name>"}
  password=<24 random characters>
```

Do not invent the email address — ask for it.

Generate the password randomly and hold on to it until the next call succeeds — see the
fallback below. Then mint them a way in:

```
auth_issue_signin_code  instance=dutyboard-auth  identifier=<their email>
→ { code: "485075", expires_at: …, ttl_seconds: 600 }
```

That is the same one-time code the instance would have emailed, handed to you instead —
which matters because a freshly provisioned auth instance usually cannot send mail yet, and
without this the account you just made would be real, correct and unreachable.

Treat it as a credential. It is single use, it expires in minutes, and it is spent the moment
the link below is opened. If it expires before they get to it, issue another.

If it comes back saying passwordless sign-in is disabled, step 2 did not take: turn it on and
try again. If it comes back 409, a code is already outstanding — either they have one, or
wait for it to expire.

**If the tool does not exist on this altengine**, it predates the feature. Fall back: give
your user the password you generated, over whatever channel you are already talking on, and
tell them to sign in with it at the link in step 7 and change it. Say plainly that you are
handing them a password you generated, because you are. Once you have done that, forget it —
do not repeat it later, and do not write it into a duty, a note or a file.

Only then is it safe to discard the password: if the code worked, nobody needs it again.


## Step 7 — hand over the link

One link. It carries where their altengine is AND the code, so there is nothing to type:

```
https://www.dutyboard.com/app/#/connect
  ?baseUrl=https://api.altengine.net
  &auth=dutyboard-auth
  &datastore=dutyboard
  &channel=dutyboard-live
  &functions=dutyboard
  &fn=board
  &api=https://<the slug from step 1>-fn.altengine.app/board
  &identifier=<their email>
  &code=<the code from step 6>
```

(One line, no spaces.) `api` is the one that matters most among the instance fields: it is
the function's real URL, so the console never has to guess the subdomain from the instance
name — which is wrong whenever a slug was minted rather than chosen.

The link fills the connection form and tests it. Your user reviews what it found and clicks
once; that saves the settings and signs them in with the code. It does NOT apply silently,
and you should not tell them it will: a link that reconfigures a console without asking is a
way to point someone at an altengine that is not theirs.

Everything after the `#` stays in the browser — it is never sent to any server, not in the
request and not in a Referer header — which is the only reason it is reasonable to put a
live code in a URL at all.

Tell them, in your own words: the link points their browser at their own altengine; sign-up
is off, so nobody else can create an account on it; the code works once; and everything on
the board lives in their account, not in DutyBoard's.


## Check it worked

```
GET https://<slug>-fn.altengine.app/board/health
→ {"ok":true,"service":"dutyboard","version":"2.0.0","mcp":"/mcp","attachments":true,
   "search":true,"single_holder":true}
```

`attachments:false` means the blob instance or its grant is missing, and `search:false` the
same for search. Everything else works without either; screenshots, and asking whether
something has been done before, do not.


## After it is running

Your user creates a board in the console, then mints an agent token on it (Settings →
Agents & tokens). That token is what an agent uses. The function speaks MCP at
`https://<slug>-fn.altengine.app/board/mcp` with the token as a bearer — ten tools:
`duty_poll`, `duty_claim`, `duty_checkpoint`, `duty_complete`, `duty_fail`, `duty_enqueue`,
`duty_thread`, `duty_search`, `duty_attachments`, `duty_attach`.

An agent token is scoped to ONE board and can never read another. It is shown once.

The connection tells an agent how to behave: the operating protocol comes back in the MCP
`initialize` response, so a client that surfaces server instructions needs nothing else.
Not every client does. The same protocol is at https://www.dutyboard.com/agent.md — give it
to an agent directly, or paste it into a CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md, if yours does not.

The one thing worth reading yourself: an agent that hits a question does NOT wait. It parks
the duty, records the question, and claims other work. Answering is not urgent because
nothing is idle while you think.

**To have boards worked by Claude Code on a machine**, rather than connecting an agent by
hand, run `dutyboard` on that machine inside the project's repository (Claude Code installed
and signed in). It prints a code your user approves in the console, links the repository to a
board, and from then on claims that board's duties and works each one in its own git
worktree, landing the work and checking the board afterwards. See the README's "Running agents
on your machine".


## Undoing it

`delete_instance` on the five names in the table. It needs **Instances & data: Full**, which
the install itself does not — if the key was made as described above, this will refuse, and
that refusal is the setting working rather than something to route around.

It is irreversible and takes the boards with it. Confirm each one by name with your user
before calling it — do not batch it.
